title: Felix's Starry Dreams
markdown:
The village square had its parade sparkle on early: carts of flowers, a smell of crushed stems, bunting that snapped like small flags of weather, and Felix the wolf clutching a programme as if it were a star chart. He was a junior astronomer, fur the colour of twilight, eyes full of nebulae, and this year he wanted Most Celestial Contribution. A small honour. To Felix it felt like a universe with a ribbon on it. He had set the telescope with the care other people reserved for wedding cakes.

“Just imagine, Bea,” he whispered to his flatmate. Bea the goat had a smile like a polished constellation and a nuzzle always ready. “The telescope on Jupiter. Perhaps a new twinkle.”

Bea had spent the morning tying pamphlets about the moon’s phases with the cheeriest blue ribbon. One lively stack scattered like paper birds. “Little rebels,” she chuckled, gathering them with practised ease. Therefore the pamphlets survived, if slightly creased, and Felix’s cart still looked like an invitation to look up.

The parade began. Then Bartholomew the goose arrived, dignity first, with a papier-mâché replica of the village fountain and a working water feature. Whoosh: an arc that delighted everyone. Felix’s sturdy telescope suddenly looked compact. Bartholomew’s posse, in tiny feathered hats, honked approval.

“Remarkable water management,” Felix managed.

Bartholomew nodded, regal. “One aims for grandeur. Especially for Most Delightful Display.” He surveyed Felix’s cart. “Your little star-gazer is quite… compact.”

Next came the prize pumpkin carved into the Mayor, enormous enough to make lunar phases feel like footnotes. Therefore most eyes left the pamphlets. Bea handed them out anyway. A few people took them. Most watched Bartholomew’s trained pigeons spell Congratulations across the blue.

Felix slumped. Bartholomew always did more, and louder. The award receded like a planet behind cloud.

Bea was not watching the pigeons with dismay. “More, yes. But is it us? We are not losing anything. We are broadening the perspective.”

Felix’s ears perked. “Broadening?”

“He wants Delightful Display. You want Celestial Contribution. What if everyone could see the celestial, not only you?”

Therefore Felix stopped trying to out-fountain a goose. He looked at the telescope, at Bea, at the few villagers who had paused over a moon-phase pamphlet. A warmth brighter than a distant star moved through him.

He turned to a young family with two wide-eyed children. “Excuse me. Would you add a wish to the stars? We are making a collective celestial mosaic. A sky made of everyone’s dreams.”

The children’s eyes widened further. Soon a small happy gathering formed around the cart. Felix, no longer measuring himself against papier-mâché water, explained astronomy as shared wonder. Bea, warmth first, offered spare programmes for drawings and secret thoughts. The scattered pamphlets came back as a colourful stack: scribbled stars, fantastical moon-walking, simple wishes for clear nights. Someone had drawn Jupiter with extra moons, as if generosity were a kind of science.

Bartholomew’s finale was a synchronised honking chorus. He strutted toward the judging stand. But the crowd was no longer solely his. A gentler energy had bloomed from the humble cart. Therefore the judges—a spectacled owl and a kindly plump badger—looked perplexed, then curious, and walked over.

Felix presented the new stack, a tapestry of community imagination. “We are not losing control. We are broadening the interpretation. Not only my observation. Everyone’s wonder.”

The owl and badger conferred. The owl cleared its throat. “Bartholomew’s Delightful Display was, indeed, delightful. Felix’s Celestial Contribution has captured the village’s spirit. He has illuminated not only distant stars, but the square itself.”

Felix’s jaw dropped. Bea bleated, joyful. Bartholomew, after a stunned pause, offered a surprisingly gracious nod. The minor honour felt, for a moment, like a new galaxy. Felix had not outdone the fountain. He had asked people to look up together, and the square, which had been all water-arcs and pigeons, kept a stack of wishes that would not stay tied.
